title: This Tiny Microbe Turns Into a Giant Cannibal!
summary: Have you ever seen a tiny creature turn into a monster? That's what happens to a microbe called Euplotes gigatrox. It's a single-celled protist that normally eats bacteria. But sometimes, a few of these microbes grow to more than twice their normal size and start eating their own brothers and sisters! Scientists call these big ones "supergiants." They found them in gunk scraped from an aquarium filter in Curaçao, a Caribbean island. Ben Larson, a cell biologist, discovered them. He says the change happens in steps. First, the microbe gets a big mouth. Then it starts running around like crazy. Once it catches a sibling in its huge mouth, its whole body changes and it becomes a giant cannibal. Normal-size microbes walk and swim, but the giants can only walk in circles. The giants can shrink back to normal size by splitting unevenly. A normal microbe divides once a day, but a shrinking giant can produce nine normal offspring in one day! Over five days, it can make up to 16. Scientists think studying these microbes might help us understand how simple life forms develop complex behaviors—and maybe even how many-celled life first evolved.
why_it_matters: Studying a tiny cannibal microbe might help scientists understand how cells change, which is a building block for learning about living things, including you.

background_read: Curaçao is an island in the Caribbean Sea that is part of the Kingdom of the Netherlands.
Microbes are living things too small to see without a microscope, and they live in many wet places, including aquarium filters.
Ben Larson (a scientist who studies cells) was looking at material from an aquarium filter when he noticed these unusual supergiants.
Article_Structure: WHO: Ben Larson, a cell biologist, discovered the unusual microbes
WHAT: Some Euplotes gigatrox grow giant mouths, change their whole bodies, and eat sibling microbes
WHERE: In gunk scraped from an aquarium filter in Curaçao, a Caribbean island
WHY: To understand how simple life forms develop complex behaviors and maybe how many-celled life evolved

perspectives.description: Ben Larson and other scientists are excited because these supergiants could reveal how single cells develop surprising complex behaviors.
Some researchers may be careful because this is just one microbe found in a filter, so it is unclear how much it can explain about ancient life.
Others see it as a useful example of how an ordinary cell can become a very different form under certain conditions.
